summary:
Chaitanya Asawa frames Abridge's mission as 'save lives, save time, save money,' which mirrors the three KPIs of any agentic product: quality, latency, and cost.

On quality, evals are the operating system. Every product begins with internal benchmarks and offline evaluation, then staged rollout to an alpha group of clinicians, beta testing, A/B at scale, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. Because most of the company is non-clinical, Abridge encodes clinician judgment into expert-calibrated LM judges, creating a feedback loop so anyone can hill-climb. Online signals like note edits, thumbs up/down, and star ratings add further signal. The framework applies across note generation, trial matching, coding, and clinical decision support.

Deep diving into clinical decision support, Abridge builds contextual decision support where a question like 'does this patient meet criteria for febrile neutropenia?' requires pulling prior labs from the EHR, the live conversation, and grounded clinical guidelines and journals. Evaluation is uniquely hard because the generator-verifier gap is nearly zero: a verifier strong enough to trust would itself be the generator. There is also no single correct answer, so Abridge uses multiple signals: a clinical quality judge, an adversarial/boundary judge, a clinical safety judge, and tone/style judges.

The clinical quality judge is built by having two independent physicians write rubrics of required elements for a good response, a third physician adjudicating those into one rubric, and a fourth running QA. Only then does an LM judge compare agent outputs to rubric elements via semantic match.

On cost and latency, Abridge handles roughly 100 million medical conversations a year, so they post-train smaller models per section of the clinical note (HPI, past medical history, assessment and plan) rather than running frontier intelligence end-to-end. Their bet is that a unique dataset plus a narrow enough problem can beat the frontier's rate of change. For in-visit order detection, cheap fast gates trigger heavier order-matching models only on relevant conversational events, keeping cost manageable while still matching mentioned orders against approved order sets.

sections.title: Reading the room and clinician testimonials
sections.summary: Asawa polls the audience on healthcare experience, clinical training, engineering background, and prior awareness of Abridge, then plays clinician testimonials emphasizing how the tool eliminates after-hours charting and restores presence during visits.

sections.title: Why healthcare gets dismissed as a technical domain
sections.summary: He acknowledges stigma that healthcare's tech problems are uninteresting while countering that fax-era infrastructure hides frontier AI challenges. He previews Abridge's journey from clinical documentation to clinical intelligence and the highest-stakes engineering problems inside.

sections.title: From robotics to search to healthcare
sections.summary: Asawa traces his path from Vicarious (AGI via neuroscience-inspired probabilistic graphical models and robotics) to Glean, where he spent 6.5 years scaling from 10 to over 1,100 people building workplace search. A decade-old Nature cover on AI skin-cancer detection plus a confusing hospital bill seeded his interest in healthcare.

sections.title: Costs that only go up, and the productivity paradox
sections.summary: He frames healthcare's productivity paradox (Baumol's cost disease): costs rise while productivity lags because labor cannot keep up, leaving technology underleveraged relative to other industries.

sections.title: Closures, thin margins, and clinician burnout
sections.summary: He cites hospital closures, razor-thin margins, and patient medical debt, plus a near-and-dear issue: widespread clinician burnout, with physicians often discouraging their children from entering the profession.

sections.title: The note after every visit, and pajama time
sections.summary: He explains the SOAP note structure, the ~2 hours/day clinicians spend writing them as 'pajama time' after work, and why these notes are high-stakes for both billing and the longitudinal record handed to the next clinician.

sections.title: Why documentation was the wedge
sections.summary: Documentation was a known pain point where quality finally met demand. Abridge's product scaled to 300 of the largest US hospital systems (Kaiser, Mayo, Johns Hopkins, Sutter) within 2-3 years, raising provider satisfaction, visit volume, and downstream billing/audit fidelity.

sections.title: Everything is downstream of the conversation
sections.summary: He states the company thesis: healthcare revolves around the doctor-patient conversation, with billing, trial matching, and clinical decision support all downstream. He argues the administrative machinery was built around that conversation and can now be folded back into it.

sections.title: Asking about trials and placing an order by voice
sections.summary: A recorded demo shows a physician asking Abridge by voice whether a patient is eligible for a trial and ordering an echocardiogram, then asking Abridge to prep tomorrow's charts. Asawa notes Abridge covers pre-visit discussion topics, post-visit summaries, notes, and pended orders across the entire visit.

sections.title: What context the system actually reads
sections.summary: He enumerates Abridge's three input streams: full EHR context (prior labs, prior notes), the live doctor-patient conversation where current symptoms surface, and grounded medical literature and clinical guidelines.

sections.title: Quality, latency, and cost on hard mode
sections.summary: He reframes the standard agentic KPIs. Quality must be near-absolute because errors in healthcare destroy trust irreversibly, unlike lower-stakes products. Latency matters because decisions must act during the live conversation, and cost pressure compounds across three axes simultaneously.

sections.title: Mission maps to the three agentic KPIs
sections.summary: Asawa notes Abridge's motto 'save lives, save time, save money' maps directly to the three KPIs of any agentic product: quality, latency, and cost.

sections.title: Evaluation as the operating system
sections.summary: Every product starts with internal benchmarks and offline evaluation, then staged rollout to an alpha group of trusted clinicians, beta testing, A/B at scale, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. Abridge encodes clinician judgment into expert-calibrated LM judges so non-clinicians can hill-climb. Online signals like note edits, thumbs up/down, and star ratings add further signal across note generation, trial matching, coding, and clinical decision support.

sections.title: Contextual clinical decision support
sections.summary: Abridge builds contextual decision support where a question like 'does this patient meet criteria for febrile neutropenia?' requires pulling prior labs from the EHR, the live conversation, and grounded clinical guidelines and journals. Evaluation is uniquely hard because the generator-verifier gap is nearly zero: a verifier strong enough to trust would itself be the generator, and there is no single correct response.

sections.title: Many signals layered into judges
sections.summary: To tackle the small generator-verifier gap, Abridge layers multiple specialized signals: a clinical quality judge (deep-dived next), an adversarial/boundary judge, a clinical safety judge, and tone/style judges, each covering a different aspect of the hard-to-measure response quality.

sections.title: Four physicians to build one rubric
sections.summary: The clinical quality judge cannot rely on a single golden response because many responses are correct. Instead, two independent physicians write rubrics listing required elements, a third physician adjudicates them into one rubric, and a fourth runs QA. Only then does an LM judge compare agent outputs to rubric elements via semantic match, enabling hill-climbing across models, agent architecture, and search ranking.

sections.title: Cost at 100 million conversations a year
sections.summary: Abridge handles ~100 million medical conversations a year, so they decompose the clinical note into sections (HPI, past medical history, assessment and plan) and post-train smaller models per section rather than calling a frontier model end-to-end, betting that a unique dataset plus a narrow problem can beat the frontier's rate of change.

sections.title: Smaller models per section of the note
sections.summary: The data flywheel of 100M conversations a year is a dataset nobody else holds. Where the frontier model would steamroll them, the bet is that right data plus focus on a narrow problem can beat frontier rate of change; where quality is already maxed out, smaller models reduce cost and latency.

sections.title: Catching orders spoken during a visit
sections.summary: Doctors dislike pending orders but often mention orders during visits. While listening in the visit, Abridge queues mentioned orders in the background for EHR sign-off, but uses cheap fast gates to trigger heavier order-matching models only on relevant conversational events, avoiding the cost of running heavy models every few seconds.

sections.title: Closing: healthcare needs frontier AI
sections.summary: Asawa closes by reframing healthcare as a domain that needs frontier AI and tests it at high stakes. He notes that as an engineer he once worried whether healthcare technology actually works, but Abridge has proven it at scale, and invites the audience to connect on Twitter or LinkedIn.
